title: The averaged switch model
summary: Replacing the switch pair by its average over one period turns the buck into a continuous circuit; perturbed and linearized, it gives the small-signal model.
text: To design the control we need a transfer function, but the switch turns on and off every \(T_s\) and has none. The way out is to look at the average of each quantity over one period, which varies slowly. This note does the derivation for the buck; the result is the plant of the next note . Step 1: the switched circuit Let \(q(t) \in \{0, 1\}\) be the state of the high-side switch. The switching-node voltage is \(v_{sw} = q\,v_{in}\) , and the current drawn from the input is \(i_{in} = q\,i_L\) . On the inductor, with \(R_s = R_L + R_{on}\) (in CCM there is always one switch in series with it): \[L\,\frac{di_L}{dt} = q\,v_{in} - v_o - R_s\,i_L\] Step 2: the average over one period Define the moving average \(\langle x \rangle_{T_s}(t) = \frac{1}{T_s}\int_{t - T_s}^{t} x(\tau)\,d\tau\) . The average of \(q\) is the duty ratio \(d\) . If \(v_{in}\) and \(i_L\) barely change within one period (small ripple), the average of the product is the product of the averages, and the switch pair becomes the averaged switching cell : \[\langle v_{sw} \rangle_{T_s} = d\,\langle v_{in} \rangle_{T_s}, \qquad \langle i_{in} \rangle_{T_s} = d\,\langle i_L \rangle_{T_s}\tag{1}\] ≡ Averaged switch model The averaged cell is an ideal transformer of ratio \(1 : d\) , with a variable \(d\) : the voltage comes out multiplied by \(d\) , and the input current is the inductor's multiplied by \(d\) . Power is conserved: \(\langle v_{in}\rangle\langle i_{in}\rangle = \langle v_{sw}\rangle\langle i_L\rangle\) . Replacing the cell in the circuit, the inductor equation becomes \[L\,\frac{d\langle i_L\rangle}{dt} = d\,\langle v_{in}\rangle - \langle v_o\rangle - R_s\,\langle i_L\rangle\] and the capacitor, the ESR and the load stay as before, with the averaged quantities. The ripple vanishes by construction. Step 3: the operating point In steady state, the derivatives vanish: \(\langle i_L\rangle = I_L = V_o/R\) and \(D\,V_{in} = V_o + R_s I_L\) , that is, \(D = \frac{V_o}{V_{in}}\cdot\frac{R + R_s}{R}\) , the duty ratio with losses. Step 4: perturbation Write each quantity as its operating point plus a small perturbation: \(d = D + \hat d\) , \(v_{in} = V_{in} + \hat v_{in}\) , \(i_L = I_L + \hat i_L\) , \(v_o = V_o + \hat v_o\) . The only nonlinear term is the product \(d\,v_{in}\) : \[d\,v_{in} = D V_{in} + V_{in}\,\hat d + D\,\hat v_{in} + \hat d\,\hat v_{in}\] Step 5: linearization The term \(\hat d\,\hat v_{in}\) is the product of two small perturbations and is neglected. Subtracting the operating point leaves a linear equation: \[L\,\frac{d\hat i_L}{dt} = V_{in}\,\hat d + D\,\hat v_{in} - \hat v_o - R_s\,\hat i_L\] The switching node becomes a source \(\hat v_{sw} = V_{in}\hat d + D\hat v_{in}\) that drives the LC filter. title: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
summary: In steady state, the volt-second balance on the inductor gives the buck's duty ratio, and the triangular current gives the current and voltage ripple.
text: The buck connects the switching node to the input, then to ground, and the LC filter delivers the average of that square wave to the load. This note computes the duty ratio and the ripple in steady state. It is the first step of the digital buck trail . V in Q1 Q2 L C R V out firmware HG LG PWM ADC Synchronous buck: the high-side switch conducts for D·Tₛ and the low-side switch for the rest of the period. Volt-second balance In steady state, the inductor current ends each period at the value it started with. Since \(v_L = L\,di_L/dt\) , the area of the inductor voltage over one period is zero: \[(V_{in} - V_o)\,D T_s + (-V_o)(1 - D)\,T_s = 0\] With the high-side switch closed, the inductor sees \(V_{in} - V_o\) ; with it open (and the low-side switch closed), it sees \(-V_o\) . Solving: \[D = \frac{V_o}{V_{in}}\tag{1}\] ≡ Duty ratio The duty ratio \(D\) is the fraction of the switching period \(T_s = 1/f_s\) during which the high-side switch conducts. We write \(D' = 1 - D\) for the rest of the period. The resistive losses ( \(R_s = R_L + R_{on}\) , in series with the inductor) call for slightly more \(D\) , because part of the voltage drops across them. In closed loop this does not matter: the controller finds the \(D\) that gives \(V_o\) on its own. Inductor current ripple During \(DT_s\) , the current rises with slope \((V_{in} - V_o)/L\) ; during \(D'T_s\) , it falls with slope \(V_o/L\) . The peak-to-peak ripple is \[\Delta i_L = \frac{(V_{in} - V_o)\,D}{L\,f_s} = \frac{V_o\,(1 - D)}{L\,f_s}\tag{2}\] ≡ The average of \(i_L\) is the load current \(I_o = V_o/R\) , because in steady state the capacitor accumulates no charge. The peak, \(I_o + \Delta i_L/2\) , is what saturates the core and what the switches must withstand. The boundary of continuous conduction Continuous conduction mode (CCM) In CCM, the inductor current never rests at zero during the period. The boundary is \(I_o = \Delta i_L/2\) : below it, the valley of the triangular wave would reach zero. In a buck with a diode, below the boundary the diode blocks and the converter enters discontinuous conduction (DCM), with another duty ratio and other dynamics. The synchronous buck is different: the low-side switch conducts in both directions, the current goes negative in the valley and the converter stays in CCM, called forced CCM. The equations of this note hold at any load. Negative current in the synchronous buck At light load, or in a downward reference step, the negative current returns energy to the input. A bench supply that cannot sink current may see its voltage rise. Controllers with "diode emulation" turn the low-side switch off when the current reaches zero, and the converter then enters DCM again. Output voltage ripple The capacitor absorbs the AC part of \(i_L\) , a triangle of \(\pm\Delta i_L/2\) . title: The ESR zero
summary: The output capacitor's series resistance adds a zero to the plant; with electrolytics it helps the loop, with ceramics it lies above the switching frequency and does not count.
text: A real capacitor has an equivalent series resistance (ESR). In the buck's plant , it appears as the factor \(1 + s/\omega_{\mathrm{ESR}}\) in the numerator of (1) : a real zero in the left half-plane. \[G_{vd}(s) = \frac{\hat v_o(s)}{\hat d(s)} = V_{in}\,\frac{R}{R + R_s}\;\frac{1 + s/\omega_{\mathrm{ESR}}}{1 + \dfrac{s}{Q\,\omega_0} + \dfrac{s^2}{\omega_0^2}}\tag{1}\] ≡ \[f_{\mathrm{ESR}} = \frac{1}{2\pi\,R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\,C}\tag{2}\] ≡ Where the zero comes from The impedance of the capacitor with its ESR is \[Z_C(s) = R_{\mathrm{ESR}} + \frac{1}{sC} = \frac{1 + s R_{\mathrm{ESR}} C}{sC}\] Below \(f_{\mathrm{ESR}}\) , \(1/sC\) dominates, and the capacitor filters. Above it, \(R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\) dominates, and the capacitor becomes a resistor: the current ripple now produces a proportional voltage ripple, the \(R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\Delta i_L\) part of equation Output voltage ripple of the buck . ESR zero The ESR zero is the frequency at which the two parts of the capacitor's impedance have equal magnitude. Above it, the buck's plant falls 20 dB per decade instead of 40, and the phase rises by up to 90° relative to the pole pair alone. What the zero does on the Bode plot A left-half-plane zero lifts the phase: \(\arctan(f/f_{\mathrm{ESR}})\) , which is 45° at \(f_{\mathrm{ESR}}\) and almost nothing a decade below. If the zero is near the crossover \(f_c\) , it supplies for free part of the phase boost the compensator would have to give. That was the case in older bucks with electrolytic capacitors, whose ESR is tens of milliohms: with them, a type II compensator was enough. With ceramic capacitors, the ESR drops to a few milliohms, and the zero moves up to hundreds of kHz, above \(f_s/2\) . There it does not help: the digital loop does not even see frequencies above \(f_s/2\) (see Sampling and the zero-order hold (ZOH) ), and the compensator must give all the phase boost, with two zeros, like the The 2p2z compensator . Do not count on the ESR An electrolytic's ESR varies with temperature (it may double in the cold) and grows with aging. A design that relies on the ESR zero for its phase margin may lose it in winter or after a few years. And putting a ceramic in parallel, to lower the ripple, moves the zero and changes the whole plant. ESR on purpose A resistor is sometimes added in series with the capacitor just to create the zero. It works, but the cost shows in the output ripple and in the load-step response, which gains an instantaneous jump of \(\Delta I\cdot R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\) . In the converters In the lab's buck, C = 47 µF with an ESR of 5 mΩ: \[f_{\mathrm{ESR}} = \frac{1}{2\pi\cdot 5\,\text{m}\Omega\cdot 47\,\text{µF}} = 677\ \text{kHz}\] That is 3.4 times the 200 kHz switching frequency. At 8 kHz, the 2p2z's crossover, the zero gives 0.7° of phase; even at \(f_s/2\) = 100 kHz it gives only 8.4°. For the loop, the capacitor is ideal, and the compensator does all the work. title: Four-switch buck-boost
summary: Two legs and one inductor that step the voltage down or up; the buck, boost and buck-boost modes, the plant that changes with the input and the mode the lab uses.
text: An 8 to 16 V battery feeding a 12 V bus must step the voltage down and up. The four-switch buck-boost does both with a single inductor, without inverting the output: a buck leg at the input (Q1 on top, Q2 below, node A) and a boost leg at the output (Q3 on top, Q4 below, node B), with the inductor between the two nodes. V in Q1 Q2 L Q3 Q4 C R V out firmware G1 G2 G2 G1 PWM ADC The lab's four-switch buck-boost: the input leg (Q1, Q2) and the output leg (Q3, Q4), with the inductor between nodes A and B. Three modes Buck. Q3 stays on and Q4 off; only the input leg switches. It is a buck: \(V = D\,V_{in}\) , the inductor current is the load's, and the plant has no right-half-plane zero. Boost. Q1 stays on and Q2 off; only the output leg switches. It is a boost: \(V = V_{in}/(1 - D)\) , with the right-half-plane zero . Buck-boost. Both legs switch together: G1 turns on Q1 and Q4, and the inductor receives the input; G2 turns on Q2 and Q3, and the inductor discharges into the output. From the volt-second balance, \(D\,V_{in} = D'\,V\) , that is, \(V/V_{in} = D/D'\) . The first two modes have lower losses, but the firmware must decide which mode it is in and switch modes when \(V_{in}\) crosses \(V\) , where each one's duty reaches its limit. The third covers the whole range with a single duty, without transitions. The price is that all four switches commutate every period and the inductor carries the input and output currents added together, \(I = I_o/D'\) . The lab's mode The lab's converter always runs in buck-boost mode: G1 drives Q1 and Q4, G2 drives Q2 and Q3. The firmware is the same as the buck's and the boost's, with one duty and one voltage loop. The small-signal model and every number on this site are for that mode. The plant in buck-boost mode With G1, the inductor sees \(+v_{in}\) ; with G2, \(-v\) . The averaged cell becomes \(L\,di_L/dt = d\,v_{in} - d'\,v - R_l\,i_L\) , and the capacitor receives \(d'\,i_L\) , as in the boost. Linearizing with \(\hat v_{in} = 0\) , \(\hat d\) switches the voltage \(V_{in} + V\) across the inductor, instead of the boost's \(V\) : \[G_{vd}(s) = Z_o(s)\,\frac{D'(V_{in} + V) - I\,(sL + R_l)}{sL + R_l + D'^2 Z_o(s)}, \qquad Z_o(s) = R \parallel \left(R_{ESR} + \frac{1}{sC}\right)\tag{1}\] ≡ Here \(R_l\) adds the inductor and the two switches always in series with it. The right-half-plane zero has the same origin as in the boost, the \(I(sL + R_l)\) term: \[\omega_{\mathrm{RHP}} = \frac{D'(V_{in} + V) - I R_l}{I L} \approx \frac{R\,D'^2}{L}\cdot\frac{V_{in} + V}{V}\tag{2}\] ≡ As in the boost, the resonance is that of the inductor seen through \(D'\) , \(f_0 \approx D'/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})\) . title: Sizing L and C
summary: How to choose the buck's inductor and capacitor from the ripple specifications, the capacitor's RMS current and the load step.
text: This procedure uses the equations of Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM backwards: it starts from the specifications and arrives at L and C. At the end, we check the lab's buck. 1. Choose the current ripple and compute L Define the relative ripple \(r = \Delta i_L / I_{o,\max}\) . Values from 20 % to 40 % are the usual starting point: less calls for a large, slow inductor; more raises the peak, the core losses and the capacitor's RMS current. From the ripple equation , \[L = \frac{V_o\,(1 - D)}{r\,I_{o,\max}\,f_s}\] Use the highest input voltage: \(1 - D\) grows with \(V_{in}\) , and so does the ripple. Saturation Check the peak \(I_{o,\max} + \Delta i_L/2\) against the inductor's saturation current, not only against its rated current. The inductance of many powdered-iron inductors drops 20 % to 30 % with current, and the ripple rises in the same proportion. 2. Compute C and the maximum ESR from the voltage ripple With the specified output ripple \(\Delta v_o\) , split the budget between the two parts: \[C \ge \frac{\Delta i_L}{8\,f_s\,\Delta v_o}, \qquad R_{\mathrm{ESR}} \le \frac{\Delta v_o}{\Delta i_L}\] With ceramic capacitors, the ESR is a few milliohms and the capacitive part dominates. With electrolytics, the ESR usually dominates, and the capacitance ends up well above the minimum. Remember that the parts are out of phase: requiring each one below \(\Delta v_o\) already leaves some margin. Ceramic capacitance under bias An X5R or X7R ceramic loses a good part of its capacitance with the applied DC voltage. Use the manufacturer's curve at the output voltage, not the rated value. 3. Check the capacitor's RMS current The buck's output capacitor carries the triangular part of \(i_L\) : \[I_{C,\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{\Delta i_L}{\sqrt{12}}\tag{1}\] ≡ Compare it with the capacitor's rated RMS current (or that of the bank), at the working temperature. 4. Check the load step and the resonance Ripple rarely sets C. In a load step \(\Delta I\) , the capacitor supplies the difference until the loop reacts, and the loop reacts in about \(1/(2\pi f_c)\) . A first-order estimate of the dip is \[\Delta V \approx \frac{\Delta I}{2\pi\,f_c\,C}\] where \(f_c\) is the crossover frequency of the loop gain . Finally, compute the resonance \(f_0 = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})\) of the plant : it must lie well below \(f_s/2\) and preferably below \(f_c\) , because the compensator will have to cancel its pole pair. 5. summary: In the boost and the buck-boost, raising the duty first pulls the output down; this right-half-plane zero, at R·D'²/L, limits the crossover frequency.
text: In the buck, raising the duty raises the voltage applied to the LC filter, and the output rises. In the boost, the same action has two opposite effects. The main switch stays on longer, the inductor builds up more current, and the output will rise; but while the switch is on, the inductor is cut off from the output. At first, the inductor current is still the same, but it reaches the output during a smaller fraction of the period, \(D' - \hat d\) : the output receives \(I\hat d\) less and falls. Only later, when the inductor current grows, does it rise. A response that starts in the opposite direction to where it ends is the signature of a right-half-plane zero . The boost's plant From the averaged model in continuous conduction, with the losses \(R_l\) of the inductor and one switch, the capacitor with its ESR and the load \(R\) , the transfer function from the duty to the output is \[G_{vd}(s) = Z_o(s)\,\frac{D' V - I\,(sL + R_l)}{sL + R_l + D'^2 Z_o(s)}, \qquad Z_o(s) = R \parallel \left(R_{ESR} + \frac{1}{sC}\right)\tag{1}\] ≡ The numerator vanishes when \(D'V = I(sL + R_l)\) . With \(I = V/(RD')\) , the inductor current, the zero sits at \(s = +\omega_{\mathrm{RHP}}\) : \[\omega_{\mathrm{RHP}} = \frac{R\,D'^2 - R_l}{L} \approx \frac{R\,D'^2}{L}\tag{2}\] ≡ Right-half-plane zero A zero at \(s = +\omega_z\) , with \(\omega_z > 0\) . Like an ordinary zero, it makes the magnitude rise by 20 dB per decade above \(\omega_z\) ; but, like a pole, it lags the phase by up to \(90^\circ\) . In a step, it makes the response start in the wrong direction. Why it limits the crossover An ordinary zero in the left half-plane helps the compensator: it gives gain and phase lead. The right-half-plane zero gives the gain and takes the phase, like a delay. The compensator cannot cancel it, because that would take a pole in the right half-plane, an unstable controller. What is left is to cross well below it: at \(f_c\) , it already takes \(\arctan(f_c/f_{\mathrm{RHP}})\) , and this lag adds to the firmware's ( Computation and PWM delay ). A common rule is to keep \(f_c\) below \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}/5\) in the worst case. And the worst case is the maximum load with the minimum input: smaller \(R\) and \(D'\) , lower zero. Unlike the buck's, the boost's plant changes a lot with the operating point, and the margins must be checked at all of them ( Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins ). loading the figure… Loop gain of the boost with the 2p2z: the crossover stays at 1.5 kHz, well below the right-half-plane zero More gain does not make the boost faster With a slow boost, the temptation is to raise the gain. title: Transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\) of the boost
summary: The boost's plant in CCM has a DC gain of about V/D', a pair of poles that comes down with D' and a right-half-plane zero; the ADC also sees an ESR term and the firmware's delay.
text: In the buck, the duty only multiplies the input, and the plant is \(V_{in}\) times the LC filter ( The buck's transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\) ). In the boost, the averaged cell multiplies the state variables: the switch node is \(d'\,v\) and the current delivered to the output is \(d'\,i_L\) , with \(d' = 1 - d\) ( The averaged switch model ). The plant inherits three differences from this: the gain depends on \(D'\) , so does the resonance, and a right-half-plane zero appears. From the averaged model to the plant With \(R_l\) the inductor's resistance plus one switch's, the averaged equations of the inductor and the capacitor, perturbed and linearized with \(\hat v_{in} = 0\) , become \[(sL + R_l)\,\hat i_L = V\hat d - D'\hat v, \qquad \hat v = Z_o\,(D'\,\hat i_L - I\,\hat d)\] with \(Z_o = R \parallel (R_{ESR} + 1/sC)\) and \(I\) the average inductor current. The first term of each equation comes from \(d\) multiplying \(v\) and \(i_L\) : these are the \(V\hat d\) and \(I\hat d\) terms the buck does not have. Eliminating \(\hat i_L\) : \[G_{vd}(s) = Z_o(s)\,\frac{D' V - I\,(sL + R_l)}{sL + R_l + D'^2 Z_o(s)}, \qquad Z_o(s) = R \parallel \left(R_{ESR} + \frac{1}{sC}\right)\tag{1}\] ≡ DC gain, resonance and Q At \(s = 0\) , \(Z_o = R\) and, without losses, \(G_{vd}(0) = V/D'\) . At 48 V with \(D' \approx 0.25\) , that gives about 190 V per unit of duty: eight times the gain of the lab's buck. The denominator is the LC filter with the inductor seen through \(D'^2\) , as an inductance \(L/D'^2\) . The pair of poles lies at \[\omega_0 \approx \frac{D'}{\sqrt{LC}}, \qquad Q \approx \frac{\omega_0}{1/(RC) + R_l/L},\] and comes down when the input falls and \(D'\) shrinks. The damping comes from the load, \(1/(RC)\) , and from the losses, \(R_l/L\) . Effective inductance In the boost's averaged model, the inductor \(L\) seen from the output is \(L/D'^2\) . With \(D' = 0.25\) , the lab's 33 µH behave as 530 µH in the output filter: the resonance is four times lower than \(1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})\) . title: The buck's transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\)
summary: The buck's plant in CCM, from duty ratio to output voltage, is a second-order system with the LC resonance, a load-dependent Q and the ESR zero.
text: The linearized averaged model replaced the switch pair by a source \(\hat v_{sw} = V_{in}\,\hat d\) that drives the output filter. The plant is therefore \(V_{in}\) times that filter's transfer function. From the circuit to the transfer function The inductor and the series resistance form \(Z_L = sL + R_s\) , with \(R_s = R_L + R_{on}\) . The capacitor with its ESR, in parallel with the load, forms \(Z_o = (R_{\mathrm{ESR}} + 1/sC)\parallel R\) . The plant is a voltage divider: \[G_{vd}(s) = V_{in}\,\frac{Z_o}{Z_L + Z_o} = V_{in}\,\frac{R\,(1 + s R_{\mathrm{ESR}} C)}{\alpha_2 s^2 + \alpha_1 s + \alpha_0}\] with \[\alpha_2 = LC\,(R + R_{\mathrm{ESR}}), \qquad \alpha_0 = R + R_s\] \[\alpha_1 = L + C\left[R R_{\mathrm{ESR}} + R_s(R + R_{\mathrm{ESR}})\right]\] Arranged in the canonical second-order form: \[G_{vd}(s) = \frac{\hat v_o(s)}{\hat d(s)} = V_{in}\,\frac{R}{R + R_s}\;\frac{1 + s/\omega_{\mathrm{ESR}}}{1 + \dfrac{s}{Q\,\omega_0} + \dfrac{s^2}{\omega_0^2}}\tag{1}\] ≡ It has three ingredients: the DC gain \(V_{in}R/(R + R_s) \approx V_{in}\) , the LC's complex pole pair and the ESR zero. The resonance and the Q The pole pair sits at the filter's resonance, with a quality factor set by the damping: \[f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}, \qquad Q \approx \frac{1}{\dfrac{Z_0}{R} + \dfrac{R_s + R_{\mathrm{ESR}}}{Z_0}}, \qquad Z_0 = \sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}\tag{2}\] ≡ Quality factor \(Q\) measures how lightly damped the pole pair is. On the Bode plot, the magnitude rises about \(20\log_{10} Q\) dB above the DC gain at \(f_0\) , and the phase drops 180° over a band about \(f_0/Q\) wide. In time, the response rings at \(f_0\) and decays with a time constant \(2Q/\omega_0\) . Two sources of damping add like conductances: the load in parallel with the capacitor, with \(Q_R = R/Z_0\) , and the series resistances, with \(Q_s = Z_0/(R_s + R_{\mathrm{ESR}})\) . Hence the dependence on the load: heavy load (small R) damps more, and \(Q\) falls; light load (large R) damps less, and \(Q\) rises up to the limit \(Z_0/(R_s + R_{\mathrm{ESR}})\) , set by the losses alone; the DC gain and \(f_0\) barely change with the load. Above \(f_0\) , the magnitude falls 40 dB per decade and the phase stays near −180°. This is the phase the compensator must lift, with zeros near the resonance, for there to be phase margin at crossover (see Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins and The 2p2z compensator ). loading the figure… The buck's plant: resonant peak near 5 kHz and a 40 dB per decade roll-off; the phase includes the digital loop's (1+D)Tₛ delay. The peak depends on the load Design the compensator at the lightest load the converter will see. That is where the resonant peak is highest, and where the loop gain may cross 0 dB again with little phase. The ESR zero The factor \(1 + s/\omega_{\mathrm{ESR}}\) in the numerator is the ESR zero : above \(f_{\mathrm{ESR}}\) , the capacitor becomes a resistor, and the magnitude stops falling at 40 dB per decade. summary: The buck's complete interrupt: read the ADC, compute the error, run the 2p2z difference equation, saturate and write the CCR, in float and in fixed point, with the cycle budget and how to measure it.
text: This note puts together everything the trail has built. The 2p2z compensator becomes the difference equation below, the saturation of Anti-windup and duty saturation sits at the output, and the arithmetic is that of Q15 fixed point : \[u[k] = -a_1\,u[k-1] - a_2\,u[k-2] + b_0\,e[k] + b_1\,e[k-1] + b_2\,e[k-2]\tag{1}\] ≡ The sequence in each period The timer reaches the end of the period and generates the update event. That event triggers the ADC. The ADC finishes the conversion and calls the interrupt. The interrupt computes the error and the new duty, and saturates it. It writes the CCR. With preload on, the new value only takes effect in the next period. Step 4 is what scenario.cpp imitates with s->duty = s->pending : the duty computed from period \(k\) 's sample governs period \(k+1\) . With trailing-edge PWM, the edge that matters comes \(D\,T_s\) into that period, and the total delay is \((1 + D)\,T_s\) , the subject of Computation and PWM delay . Float variant (Cortex-M4F, M33) This is scenario.cpp 's logic, with the error in volts and the coefficients of the buck's default design. title: The 2p2z compensator
summary: The two-pole, two-zero compensator, a digital relative of the type III, designed by its poles and zeros, and its relation with the PID; with the buck's default design.
text: The buck's plant, above the LC resonance, has a phase near \(-180^\circ\) ( The buck's transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\) ), and the digital delay takes even more ( Computation and PWM delay ). An integrator alone would add \(-90^\circ\) , and the loop would have no margin. The compensator needs an integrator, to drive the steady-state error to zero, and two zeros, to give phase back at the crossover. That is the 2p2z : two poles, two zeros. \[C(z) = K\,\frac{(1 - z_1 z^{-1})(1 - z_2 z^{-1})}{(1 - z^{-1})(1 - p\,z^{-1})}, \qquad z_i = e^{-\omega_{zi} T_s}, \quad p = e^{-\omega_p T_s}\tag{1}\] ≡ The two poles are the integrator, at \(z = 1\) , and a real high-frequency pole \(p\) . It is the digital version of the analog type III compensator, which has two high-frequency poles instead of one. Design by poles and zeros Each root has a job, and the design is done on the Bode plot of the loop gain : Integrator ( \(z = 1\) ): infinite gain at DC, zero steady-state error at the sample. Two zeros near or below the LC resonance: each gives back up to \(+90^\circ\) . Below the resonance, they already give almost all their lead when the plant's phase plunges. Lower zeros give more phase at \(f_c\) , but they lower the gain between the integrator and the resonance, and the loop becomes slow to correct errors in that band. High-frequency pole : limits the gain above the crossover, where there is only ripple and quantization noise ( ADC quantization ). When the ESR zero falls inside the band, the pole is placed on it to cancel it ( The ESR zero ). Gain \(K\) : chosen last, so that \(|T_L| = 1\) at \(f_c\) . The zeros and the pole go to \(z\) by matching ( The bilinear (Tustin) transform and prewarping ): \(z_i = e^{-\omega_{zi}T_s}\) and \(p = e^{-\omega_p T_s}\) . Expanding the numerator and the denominator, \[C(z) = \frac{b_0 + b_1 z^{-1} + b_2 z^{-2}}{1 + a_1 z^{-1} + a_2 z^{-2}},\] the firmware receives \(b_0 = K\) , \(b_1 = -K(z_1+z_2)\) , \(b_2 = K z_1 z_2\) , \(a_1 = -(1+p)\) and \(a_2 = p\) , and runs the difference equation \[u[k] = -a_1\,u[k-1] - a_2\,u[k-2] + b_0\,e[k] + b_1\,e[k-1] + b_2\,e[k-2]\tag{2}\] ≡ This is the velocity form : the integrator lives in the two past \(u\) terms. Since the integrator at \(z = 1\) forces \(1 + a_1 + a_2 = 0\) , the equation can be rewritten as \(u[k] - u[k-1] = a_2\,(u[k-1] - u[k-2]) + b_0\,e[k] + b_1\,e[k-1] + b_2\,e[k-2]\) : the firmware computes the increment \(\Delta u\) and adds it to the previous duty. The code is in The 2p2z in C, in the interrupt ; what happens when \(u\) saturates, in Anti-windup and duty saturation . loading the figure… Poles and zeros of the buck's 2p2z in the z-plane: integrator at z = 1, double zeros near 1, pole near the origin The relation with the PID In \(s\) , the prototype is \[C(s) = K_I\,\frac{(1 + s/\omega_{z1})(1 + s/\omega_{z2})}{s\,(1 + s/\omega_p)} = K_P + \frac{K_I}{s} + \frac{K_D\,s}{1 + s\,T_F},\] a PID with a filter on the derivative. title: ADC quantization
summary: The ADC reads the output in steps of \(q = V_{FS}/(2^N - 1)\): the step, the quantization noise, the reference written as a code and the sampling instant decide what the loop can regulate.
text: The digital controller doesn't see the output voltage: it sees an integer. In Sampling and the zero-order hold (ZOH) , sampling made time discrete; here the A/D converter (ADC) makes the amplitude discrete, and everything the firmware knows about \(v_o\) goes through that rounding. The step (LSB) ADC step The step, or LSB (least significant bit), is the smallest change of the measured voltage that changes the code read. An \(N\) -bit ADC has \(2^N\) codes, from 0 to \(2^N - 1\) : code 0 reads 0 V, the largest reads full scale, and between them the measuring range is divided into \(2^N - 1\) steps. The ADC pin only accepts 0 to \(V_{\mathrm{ADC}}\) (3.3 V on an STM32). To measure a larger output, a resistive divider of ratio \(k_{\mathrm{div}}\) scales the voltage down, and the range referred to the output becomes \(V_{FS} = V_{\mathrm{ADC}}/k_{\mathrm{div}}\) : \[q = \frac{V_{FS}}{2^{N} - 1} = \frac{V_{\mathrm{ADC}}}{(2^{N} - 1)\,k_{\mathrm{div}}}\tag{1}\] ≡ In the buck, \(V_{FS}\) = 20 V and \(N\) = 12 bits. The divider has \(k_{\mathrm{div}} = 3.3/20 = 0.165\) , and \[q = \frac{20\ \text{V}}{4095} = 4.884\ \text{mV at the output} \qquad \left(\frac{3.3\ \text{V}}{4095} = 0.806\ \text{mV at the pin}\right).\] Code \(k\) reads \(k \cdot 20/4095\) V: the largest, 4095, reads exactly 20 V. That is the scale of the simulations' firmware ( scenario.cpp ), which rounds the sample to the nearest code. The range needs headroom above the nominal output, to see the overshoot and to protect against overvoltage, but every volt of headroom makes \(q\) coarser. Quantization noise When the voltage moves many steps between samples, the rounding error \(\varepsilon = v - q\cdot\text{code}\) spreads evenly between \(-q/2\) and \(q/2\) . The variance of that uniform distribution is \[\sigma_\varepsilon^2 = \frac{1}{q}\int_{-q/2}^{q/2} \varepsilon^2\, d\varepsilon = \frac{q^2}{12}, \qquad \sigma_\varepsilon = \frac{q}{\sqrt{12}} \approx 0.29\,q .\] In the buck, \(\sigma_\varepsilon = 4.884/\sqrt{12} = 1.41\) mV rms. This white-noise model holds during transients. In steady state it fails: the output barely changes, and the quantization error becomes a fixed error, or a repeating pattern. The same goes for a measurement: a signal that moves the sample by less than one code is lost in the rounding, which is why the sine that measures the loop gain grows with frequency ( Measuring the loop gain by injecting into the duty ). What the zero-error band means For the controller, every output within a band of width \(q\) around the reference's code gives the same error. Inside that band the integrator has nothing to correct. The regulation's resolution is, at best, \(\pm q/2 = \pm 2.44\) mV at 9 V, or 0.03 %. That is resolution, not accuracy. The divider's tolerance and the ADC's gain and offset errors are worth tens of steps (see exercise 1). title: Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost
summary: In the boost and the buck-boost, the sample taken just before G1 turns on sits above the output's average and reads an ESR term that changes the plant; with it, the effective delay that fits QSPICE is (1 + 0.6·D)·Tₛ.
text: The averaged model describes the output's average over a period. The ADC does not read the average: it reads the voltage at one instant, and what that instant sees depends on the waveform. In the buck, the sample at the start of the period falls near the ripple's valley, a few millivolts below the average ( Sampling and the zero-order hold (ZOH) ). In the boost and the buck-boost, the difference is larger and, besides, it changes with the duty and with the current: it becomes part of the plant. What the sample reads This site's firmware triggers the ADC at the start of each period, just before G1 turns on. In the boost, G1 is the main switch: until then, G2 was conducting, and the capacitor received the inductor current minus the load's. Two effects add up: The capacitor ripple. While G1 conducts, only the capacitor feeds the load, and the voltage falls by \(\Delta v_C = I_o D T_s/C\) ; while G2 conducts, it rises again. The sample catches the end of the rise, the peak: \(\Delta v_C/2\) above the average. The ESR drop. On average, the capacitor receives \(d'\,i_L - i_o = 0\) . At the sampling instant, it receives \(i_L - i_o\) : the whole inductor current, \(d\,i_L\) more than the average. The sample reads \(R_{ESR}\,d\,i_L\) more, minus the valley of the current ripple. The first effect is nearly constant and only shifts the regulated value: the loop regulates the sample, and the average sits below it. The second changes with \(d\) and with \(i_L\) , and its linearization enters the plant: \[\hat v_s = \hat v + R_{ESR}\left(D\,\hat i_L + I\,\hat d\right)\tag{1}\] ≡ Plant seen by the ADC The transfer function from the duty to the sample , not to the average output. It is the one that enters the loop gain. In this site's boost and buck-boost, it is \(G_{vd}\) plus the ESR term, times the firmware's delay. The \(R_{ESR}\,I\,\hat d\) term does not fall with frequency. Well above the resonance, the \(-I(sL + R_l)\) term leaves the average output at about \(-I\,Z_o\,\hat d\) , which includes \(-I\,R_{ESR}\,\hat d\) ; the sample cancels that part, and the right-half-plane zero moves up. The plant seen by the ADC gains a little phase near the crossover, and a design made with the average stays on the conservative side. The effective delay The delay from the sample to the edge it moves is \((1 + D)\,T_s\) in the buck ( Computation and PWM delay ). In the boost and the buck-boost, the delay that best fits the QSPICE measurements, with the ESR term already in the model, is shorter: \[t_d = (1 + 0.6\,D)\,T_s\] The 0.6 factor was found by fitting, comparing the model with the loop gain measured on the switched circuit ( Measuring the loop gain by injecting into the duty ), not derived. The firmware's delay is still \((1 + D)\,T_s\) ; the smaller factor absorbs what the averaged model, even with the ESR term, does not yet describe, and should not be read as a physical delay. title: Anti-windup and duty saturation
summary: When the duty hits its limit, the integrator must not keep accumulating error: the integrator clamp, the 2p2z velocity form, back-calculation, the reference slew and the derivative kick.
text: The duty has limits, and the linear 2p2z compensator doesn't know it. This note shows, step by step, how to keep an integrator from accumulating error while the output is saturated. 1. Saturate the duty Every controller ends with a clamp to \([d_{\min}, d_{\max}]\) . In the buck, \(d_{\min}\) = 0 and \(d_{\max}\) = 0.9. Besides the physical limit between 0 and 1, a maximum below 1 leaves time for the driver's bootstrap capacitor to recharge and an off interval to measure current. With \(d_{\max} = 0.9\) , the buck only delivers 15 V if the input is above about 17 V. 2. Understand windup While the output is saturated, the loop is open: raising the command changes nothing. The integrator keeps adding the error, and that excess must be discharged later, with an error of the opposite sign, that is, with overshoot. The PID of scenario.cpp and buck_pid.cpp uses the simplest solution, the integrator clamp : the state is limited to the same range as the duty. integ += KI * T * err; if (integ < DMIN) integ = DMIN; /* anti-windup by clamping */ if (integ > DMAX) integ = DMAX; d = KP * err + integ + deriv; if (d < DMIN) d = DMIN; if (d > DMAX) d = DMAX; The clamp prevents the worst, but the integrator can still sit at \(d_{\max}\) when the operating point needs much less, and the output overshoots the reference while it unwinds. The example at the end of section 3 measures that overshoot in the boost. 3. Or use the velocity form The 2p2z in C computes each duty from the two previous ones ( equation Difference equation of the 2p2z ) and stores the saturated ones. No state grows past the limits: the form is anti-windup by construction. It has one flaw, though. When a jump in the error saturates the duty, the next period's term \(b_1\,e[k-1]\) takes back the whole kick, which was never applied, and the duty plunges the other way. Measured in the boost: clamp versus velocity form QSPICE simulations of the boost, with the netlist and firmware of the scenarios. The same PID ( \(K_P\) = 0.0114, \(K_I\) = 18.2, \(K_D\) = 1.75 µs/V, \(T_F\) = 7.96 µs) runs with the integrator clamp and as a 2p2z in velocity form, with the same transfer function. Settling, here, means entering the ±2 % band around 48 V for good. Input dropout. At 6 V, not even \(d_{\max} = 0.85\) is enough: the output stalls at 36.6 V, and the integrator sits on the clamp at 0.85, while the operating point at 12 V needs 0.76. The input then returns to 12 V at 10 V/ms. PID with clamp: another 450 µs at the limit, 33.8 A in the inductor, a 56.0 V peak, and settling in 1.79 ms. That is windup. Velocity form: 240 µs at the limit, 21.5 A, a 50.4 V peak, and settling in 0.96 ms. Reference step from 40 to 48 V, without slew. The derivative kick takes the duty to 0.85. PID with clamp: four periods at 0.85, no overshoot, and settling in 1.0 ms. Velocity form: this is the flaw above. The duty drops to 0.09 and stays at zero for two periods, the inductor current goes to −34.7 A, and the output plunges to 7.7 V.

title: Computation and PWM delay
summary: From the ADC sample to the PWM edge it moves, \((1 + D)\,T_s\) go by in this firmware, and this delay costs \(360^\circ\, f\,(1 + D)\,T_s\) of phase at the crossover.
text: In an analog loop, a change at the output reaches the PWM comparator almost at once. In a digital one, the information travels a chain: the ADC converts, the interrupt computes, the PWM register is updated and, only then, an edge of the pulse moves. Each stage delays the response, and a pure delay \(t_d\) is \(e^{-s t_d}\) : it leaves the magnitude of the loop gain alone, but takes phase. The chain in this site's firmware Period \(k\) starts at \(t = kT_s\) : Sample and conversion. The timer triggers the ADC at \(kT_s\) ( Sampling and the zero-order hold (ZOH) ). The conversion takes from hundreds of nanoseconds to a few microseconds. Computation. The end-of-conversion interrupt runs the PID or the 2p2z and writes the new duty to the compare register (CCR). Update in the next period. With preload on, the new CCR only takes effect at the next update event, at \((k+1)T_s\) . This guarantees a whole pulse with the old value, even if the computation runs late, and costs one period. The modulated edge. In a trailing-edge (sawtooth) PWM, the switch turns on at the start of the period and off at \((k+1+D)T_s\) . Only that edge depends on \(d\) ; the duty perturbation enters the plant there, \(DT_s\) after the start. Adding up, the delay from the sample to the edge it moves is \[\varphi_d(f) = -360^\circ\, f\, t_d, \qquad t_d = (1 + D)\,T_s\tag{1}\] ≡ The \(DT_s\) term plays the role of the zero-order hold: instead of the ZOH's average half period, the modulator delays up to the edge that actually moves. The PWM modulator also has a gain: in a real timer, \(d = \mathrm{CCR}/\mathrm{ARR}\) , and an 850-step counter (170 MHz for 200 kHz) gives \(1/850\) per step. In this firmware the duty is computed per unit, the modulator's gain is 1 and \(G_{vd}\) already includes \(V_{in}\) . title: DPWM resolution and limit cycles
summary: The duty also moves in steps: when the step it causes at the output is larger than the ADC step, the loop has nowhere to settle and oscillates in a limit cycle.
text: In ADC quantization , the measurement of the output moved in steps. So does the actuator: the digital PWM (DPWM) only produces a finite number of duty values, and the two quantizers together can keep the loop from settling. The DPWM step A timer counts clock pulses from 0 to the end of the period, and the PWM output changes when the counter passes the compare value (the CCR register). The duty can only be \(\mathrm{CCR}/N_{\mathrm{PWM}}\) : \[N_{\mathrm{PWM}} = \frac{f_{\mathrm{clk}}}{f_s}, \qquad \Delta D = \frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{PWM}}}, \qquad n_{\mathrm{PWM}} = \log_2 N_{\mathrm{PWM}}\tag{1}\] ≡ On an STM32G4 with the timer at 170 MHz and \(f_s\) = 200 kHz, there are \(170/0.2 = 850\) counts per period: \(\Delta D = 1/850\) , or \(\log_2 850 = 9.7\) bits. In center-aligned mode (the counter goes up and down) 425 counts remain, 8.7 bits. The resolution gets worse with the switching frequency: doubling \(f_s\) costs one bit. High-resolution timers solve this. The STM32G4's HRTIM divides each 170 MHz cycle into 32 (184 ps steps), which is like counting at 5.44 GHz: 27,200 counts at 200 kHz, or 14.7 bits. Other manufacturers have similar peripherals. The step at the output In steady state, changing the duty by \(\Delta D\) moves the output by \(|G_{vd}(0)|\,\Delta D\) , with \(G_{vd}\) the plant of The buck's transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\) . In the buck, \(G_{vd}(0) \approx V_{in}\) : \[\Delta V_{\mathrm{DPWM}} = \frac{24\ \text{V}}{850} = 28.2\ \text{mV} \qquad \text{against} \qquad q = 4.884\ \text{mV}.\] One step of the ordinary timer moves the output almost six ADC steps. No CCR value puts the output inside the ADC's zero-error band, which is only 4.884 mV wide. loading the figure… The buck's two quantizers: a 12-bit ADC and a 10-bit DPWM (1024 counts, 23.4 mV per step at the output). Change the resolutions and see when a DPWM level appears inside the zero-error band. Limit cycle Limit cycle A sustained periodic oscillation of a nonlinear system, with no external excitation. In a quantized loop, the output alternates between DPWM levels because none of them cancels the error read. The mechanism is simple. The integrator accumulates the error and raises the duty one step; the output rises 28 mV and jumps over the band; the error changes sign, the integrator goes down, and the story repeats. The linear analysis of Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins doesn't predict it: the loop can have good margins and still oscillate, with an amplitude of the order of the DPWM step. Peterchev and Sanders (2003) gave three conditions for removing steady-state limit cycles: a DPWM finer than the ADC , so that a DPWM level exists inside the zero-error band. They suggest one extra bit, which gives two DPWM levels per ADC level; an integrator in the controller, with limited gain . title: Q15 fixed point
summary: Without an FPU, coefficients and signals become scaled integers: Qm.n formats, Q15 multiplication with rounding and saturation, and the scaling of the buck's 2p2z coefficients.
text: The 2p2z compensator has coefficients such as 0.23114 and −0.43413. With a floating-point unit, they go into the code as they are. Without one, each number becomes an integer with an implicit scale. Float or fixed point? With an FPU (Cortex-M4F, M7, M33 with FPU, such as the STM32G4, F4 and H7): use float . The single-precision FPU multiplies and adds in one to three cycles (typical datasheet figures, not measured here), and the 24-bit mantissa is more than enough for this loop. Without an FPU (Cortex-M0 and M0+, such as the STM32G0 and C0): every float operation becomes a library call of, typically, tens of cycles. With a 5 µs period and a 64 MHz core, there are only 320 cycles per period. Here fixed point is used. Hidden double precision On a single-precision FPU, 0.5 is a double , and x * 0.5 is computed in software. Write 0.5f , and compile with -Wdouble-promotion so the compiler points out the cases. The Qm.n format Qm.n format A signed integer \(X\) represents \(x = X/2^n\) : \(n\) fraction bits and \(m\) integer bits besides the sign, \(1 + m + n\) bits in all. Q15 (or Q0.15) is the int16_t read as a fraction, from −1 to \(1 - 2^{-15}\) , in steps of \(3.05\times10^{-5}\) . \[x = \frac{X}{2^{n}}, \quad X \in \left[-2^{m+n},\; 2^{m+n}-1\right], \qquad Z = \left\lfloor \frac{X\,Y + 2^{n-1}}{2^{n}} \right\rfloor\tag{1}\] ≡ Q2.13 covers −4 to 4 in steps of \(1.22\times10^{-4}\) : it trades resolution for headroom. The product of two Q15 numbers has 30 fraction bits and fits in 32 bits. To return to Q15, add half a step ( \(2^{14}\) ) and shift by 15 bits: #include <stdint.h> static inline int16_t sat16(int32_t x) /* saturate instead of wrapping */ { return x > INT16_MAX ? INT16_MAX : x < INT16_MIN ? INT16_MIN : (int16_t)x; } static inline int16_t q15_mul(int16_t a, int16_t b) { int32_t p = (int32_t)a * b; /* Q30: the cast comes before the multiplication */ p += 1 << 14; /* round instead of truncating */ return sat16(p >> 15); /* -1 * -1 = +1 doesn't fit in Q15: saturate */ } Three pitfalls Overflow: without saturation, \(0.9 + 0.2\) in Q15 becomes \(-0.9\) . A duty that jumps from 0.9 to −0.9 is the worst possible error. On the Cortex-M3 and M4, CMSIS offers __SSAT(x, 16) , which saturates in one instruction. Truncation: p >> 15 without the half step always rounds down, a bias that the integrator accumulates. Shifting negatives: in C99, >> of a negative number is implementation-defined. In GCC for ARM it is arithmetic; check your compiler. To add several products, use a 64-bit accumulator. Each Q15 × Q15 product already takes 31 bits, and two of them added can overflow 32 bits. On the Cortex-M4, the SMLAL instruction multiplies and accumulates in 64 bits in one cycle, according to the core's manual. The M0 has no such instruction, and the compiler emulates the operation with several. title: Measuring the loop gain by injecting into the duty
summary: A sine added to the duty in the firmware gives the loop gain as \(-C/U\); the amplitude has to grow with frequency so the ADC sample moves several codes, and a second measurement at half the amplitude shows whether the point is linear.
text: The site's models were checked against the switched circuit in QSPICE, with the scenarios' firmware. This note shows how: where the sine goes in, how the loop gain comes out, and the two precautions that separate a reliable measurement from one that only measures the ADC's rounding. The injection Inside the interrupt, the firmware adds a small sine \(x\) to the duty \(c\) the controller computed, and the PWM uses \(u = c + x\) . The sine goes around the loop: it moves the output, the ADC sample, the error and, one period later, \(c\) itself. With \(T_L = G_c\,G_{vd}\,H\) and the error defined as reference minus sample, the part of \(c\) at the sine's frequency is \(\hat c = -T_L\,\hat u\) , and \[T_L = -\frac{C}{U},\] with \(C\) and \(U\) the Fourier components of \(c\) and \(u\) at the injected frequency. Since both signals are read at the same point in the firmware, the computation and PWM delays enter the measurement with no extra care. The same computation with the sample \(V\) in place of \(C\) gives the plant as the ADC sees it, \(V/U\) , without the compensator. In the lab, tools/qspice_loop_check.py records \(c\) , \(u\) and the sample every period, waits 30 ms for the LC resonance, which rings for tens of milliseconds in open loop, and computes \(C\) and \(U\) over 40 whole cycles of the sine, with a Hann window against the leakage of that ringing. On a board, the procedure is the same: the firmware injects and records \(c\) and \(u\) , and the computation is done offline. The amplitude grows with frequency The sine has to be small so as not to leave the linear regime, but the ADC sample only moves in steps of \(q = V_{FS}/(2^N - 1)\) ( ADC quantization ). Above the resonance, the plant falls, and a fixed amplitude that is enough at low frequency ends up moving the sample by less than one code: what gets measured then is the rounding, not the plant. The way out is to choose, at each frequency, the amplitude that, according to the model, moves the sample by about 10 codes: \[a(f) = \min\!\left(0.06,\ \max\!\left(0.004,\ \frac{10\,q}{|P(f)|}\right)\right),\] with \(P\) the plant from the duty to the sample, in volts per unit of duty. The floor, 0.004, keeps the sine small near the resonance, where a large one would reverse the inductor current at light load; the ceiling is 0.06, or less when the applied duty, which swings by \(a/|1+T_L|\) , would come close to its limits: it may use at most 80 % of its distance to \(D_{min}\) or \(D_{max}\) . In the boost at 10 V input, from 5.5 to 7 kHz, 0.06 would take the duty to 0.87, above the 0.85 limit. The linearity check In a linear system, the gain does not depend on the amplitude. So each frequency is measured again with half the sine: if \(T_L\) changes by more than 0.5 dB or 3°, the point is not linear and must not be used to check the model. title: Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins
summary: The loop gain \(T_L = G_c\,G_{vd}\,H\), the crossover frequency and the phase and gain margins, and what they predict about overshoot and ringing.
text: A voltage loop reads the output, compares it with the reference and corrects the duty. If we open the loop at any point and follow a signal once around it, it goes through three blocks in series: the controller \(G_c\) , the plant \(G_{vd}\) from the small-signal note and the sensor \(H\) . Their product is the loop gain : \[G_{vd}(s) = \frac{\hat v_o(s)}{\hat d(s)} = V_{in}\,\frac{R}{R + R_s}\;\frac{1 + s/\omega_{\mathrm{ESR}}}{1 + \dfrac{s}{Q\,\omega_0} + \dfrac{s^2}{\omega_0^2}}\tag{1}\] ≡ \[T_L(s) = G_c(s)\,G_{vd}(s)\,H\tag{2}\] ≡ Loop gain \(T_L(s)\) is the gain of a signal that goes once around the loop. With the loop closed, the output follows the reference by \(T_L/(1+T_L)\) , and a disturbance at the output is divided by \(1 + T_L\) . Where \(|T_L| \gg 1\) , the output follows the reference; where \(|T_L| \ll 1\) , the loop does nothing. Stability is analyzed on \(T_L\) , not on the closed loop. Crossover and margins Crossover frequency \(f_c\) : where \(|T_L| = 1\) (0 dB). In order of magnitude, it is the closed loop's bandwidth; the higher it is, the faster the loop corrects. Phase margin (PM): \(180^\circ + \angle T_L(j2\pi f_c)\) . It is how much extra phase lag the loop still tolerates at \(f_c\) before it oscillates. Gain margin (GM): \(-|T_L|_{\mathrm{dB}}\) at the frequency where the phase crosses \(-180^\circ\) . It is how much the gain can still rise. Both measure the distance from \(T_L\) to the point \(-1\) , where \(1 + T_L = 0\) and the loop oscillates by itself. At the crossover, \(|1 + T_L| = 2\sin(\mathrm{PM}/2)\) , so the closed loop peaks near \(f_c\) at about \[\left|\frac{T_L}{1+T_L}\right|_{f_c} = \frac{1}{2\sin(\mathrm{PM}/2)}.\] That is what the margin predicts in the time domain: with a PM of 60° there is no peak, the overshoot is small and a step settles in a few cycles of \(f_c\) . With 30°, the peak is already close to 6 dB, and every step rings at a frequency near \(f_c\) . A rough rule for the damping of the dominant pair is \(\zeta \approx \mathrm{PM}/100\) . loading the figure… Loop gain of the buck with the default 2p2z: crossover, phase margin and gain margin Why \(f_c\) cannot rise at will Three things limit the crossover of a converter controlled by a microcontroller: Sampling. The firmware sees the output once per period ( Sampling and the zero-order hold (ZOH) ). Nothing above \(f_s/2\) can be controlled, and well before that the averaged model loses accuracy. Delay. The duty computed from a sample only moves the output \((1+D)\,T_s\) later ( Computation and PWM delay ). This delay leaves \(|T_L|\) alone, but takes a phase that grows linearly with \(f\) . Above the LC resonance, the buck's phase is already near \(-180^\circ\) , and the compensator only gives back a limited lead ( The 2p2z compensator ). So, in practice, \(f_c\) seldom goes above \(f_s/10\) ; the buck's 2p2z crosses at \(f_s/25\) . title: Robust design across the operating range
summary: One fixed compensator for a plant that changes with the input and the load: the corners of the range, the crossover below about 1/5 of the right-half-plane zero in the worst case, and the margins checked at every point.
text: In the buck, the plant hardly changes with the load, and one design point is enough ( The buck's transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\) ). In the boost and the buck-boost, the resonance, the gain above it and the right-half-plane zero depend on \(D'\) and on the current ( Transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\) of the boost , Four-switch buck-boost ). The firmware has a single compensator, with fixed coefficients. This note shows how to choose that compensator so that it works across the whole range. 1. List the corners of the range The plant changes with the input and with the load, and the extremes of each form the corners: minimum and maximum input, minimum and maximum load. Add the nominal point, where the gain will be tuned. The margins are computed at all these points, at the end. 2. Find the worst right-half-plane zero The zero comes down when the load rises and when the input falls ( equation Right-half-plane zero of the boost ; in the buck-boost, equation Right-half-plane zero of the buck-boost ). The worst case is the minimum input with the maximum load . That zero, not the nominal point's, limits the crossover. 3. Choose the crossover At \(f_c\) , the zero takes \(\arctan(f_c/f_{\mathrm{RHP}})\) of phase, and the firmware's delay takes \(360^\circ\,f_c\,t_d\) ( Computation and PWM delay ). The common rule is \(f_c \le f_{\mathrm{RHP,min}}/5\) : with it, the zero costs at most 11°. It is a starting point, and what decides is the phase budget of the loop gain at the worst corner. 4. Place the zeros and the pole The two zeros of the 2p2z go below the lowest resonance of the range, so that they already give phase when the plant's phase plunges. The pole goes well above the crossover. 5. Tune the gain and follow the crossover The gain \(K\) is tuned at the nominal point. At the other points, the crossover moves. Well above the resonance, the plant's magnitude tends to \(V_{in}/(\omega^2 LC)\) in the buck, the boost and the buck-boost. In the last two, it is the DC gain, about \(V_{in}/D'^2\) , times \((f_0/f)^2\) , with \(f_0\) proportional to \(D'\) : the \(D'^2\) cancels. Higher input, higher crossover. Near the resonance, the plant lies above that asymptote, and further above the closer it is: since \(f_0\) rises with the input, the crossover rises more than the asymptote predicts. 6. Check the margins at every corner The margin of a single point misleads. A design can have a comfortable margin at light load and almost none at heavy load. The load step leads to the worst point On a load step, the converter moves precisely to the point of larger current and lower zero. title: Sampling and the zero-order hold (ZOH)
summary: The ADC reads the output once per period, at the same point of the PWM, and the computed duty is held for a whole period; this removes the ripple, creates an offset and costs half a period of phase.
text: In an analog loop, the compensator sees the output voltage all the time. In a microcontroller, the ADC takes one sample per period , triggered by the PWM's own timer, and the firmware only knows the sequence \(v[k] = v_o(kT_s)\) . On this site, the sample is taken at the start of each PWM period , just before the high-side switch turns on, and the sampling period is the switching period: \(T_s = 1/f_s\) . Nyquist A sampled sequence cannot tell a sine at \(f\) from one at \(f_s - f\) , \(f_s + f\) and so on: they all give the same samples. Only the band up to the Nyquist frequency , \(f_s/2\) , is represented without ambiguity. Any component above it shows up folded (aliased) below it, and the loop reacts to it as if it were real. That is why the site's Bode plots stop at \(f_s/2\) , and the crossover sits many times below it ( Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins ). The ripple and the offset The switching ripple is exactly at \(f_s\) and its harmonics. Sampled at \(f_s\) , it folds down to zero frequency: since the ADC always reads the same point of the period, every sample sees the same part of the ripple. The result is a smooth signal, with no ripple, which is good for control, but shifted from the average by a constant. Sampling offset It is the difference between the ripple's value at the sampling instant and the output's average. The controller's integrator drives the error of the sample to zero, so the output's average ends up shifted from the reference by this offset. In the buck, with the switch turning on at the start of the period, the inductor current is at its minimum there: the capacitor is discharging, and the ESR adds a drop. The sample reads below the average, and the output's average sits a little above the reference. The value depends on \(D\) , on the load and on any delay in the ADC trigger. Sampling near an edge On the board, right after each switching edge there are spikes and ringing of tens of MHz at the output node and in the divider. A sample at the edge can catch that noise. On microcontrollers, delay the ADC trigger a few hundred nanoseconds after the edge, or sample in the middle of the pulse, as center-aligned PWM does ( Computation and PWM delay ). The anti-aliasing filter is for those spikes, not for correcting the offset. The zero-order hold On the other side of the loop, the duty computed from \(v[k]\) stays in force for a whole period, until the next computation. A signal that jumps from value to value and stays constant between them is the output of a zero-order hold (ZOH): \[G_h(s) = \frac{1 - e^{-sT_s}}{s}, \qquad \frac{G_h(j\omega)}{T_s} = \frac{\sin(\omega T_s/2)}{\omega T_s/2}\, e^{-j\omega T_s/2}\tag{1}\] ≡ The magnitude is practically 1 well below \(f_s\) (the sinc function drops only 0.02 dB at 8 kHz with \(f_s = 200\) kHz), but the phase is \(-\omega T_s/2\) : the hold behaves as a delay of half a period . title: From the analog buck to the digital loop
summary: From the power stage to the firmware: the design path of a microcontroller-controlled buck, note by note.
text: This trail walks through the design of a buck converter controlled by a microcontroller, from the duty cycle to the interrupt's code. Follow the steps in order; the links inside each note are optional detours. The worked example is the Synchronous buck 24 V → 9 V: worked example . Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM : the starting point, the duty cycle and the ripple in steady state. Sizing L and C : from the ripple specifications, we choose L and C. The averaged switch model : to control the converter, we replace the switch by its average. The buck's transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\) : linearizing the averaged model gives the plant \(G_{vd}(s)\) . The ESR zero : the capacitor's series resistance adds a zero to the plant. Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins : plant and controller form the loop gain, and the margins tell whether the loop is stable. Sampling and the zero-order hold (ZOH) : in the microcontroller, the output is sampled and the duty cycle is held for a period. Computation and PWM delay : computing and the PWM delay the response, and the delay costs phase margin. The bilinear (Tustin) transform and prewarping : we take the controller from s to z. The 2p2z compensator : the two-pole, two-zero compensator, designed from its poles and zeros. ADC quantization : the ADC sees only steps of voltage. Measuring the loop gain by injecting into the duty : we measure the loop gain in the switched circuit, with a sine large enough to beat those steps. DPWM resolution and limit cycles : the duty cycle moves in steps too, which can cause limit cycles. Q15 fixed point : without an FPU, numbers become scaled integers. Anti-windup and duty saturation : when the duty cycle saturates, the controller must stop accumulating error. The 2p2z in C, in the interrupt : everything together, in the interrupt's C code.

title: The bilinear (Tustin) transform and prewarping
summary: How to take a controller from s to z by the trapezoidal rule, why the frequencies warp, how to correct them at the crossover, and how Tustin compares with Euler and with matched poles and zeros.
text: We design the compensator in \(s\) , with the Bode plot of the loop gain , but the firmware can only compute with samples: sums of present and past values, that is, a function of \(z\) . The exact relation is \(z = e^{sT_s}\) , but \(s = \ln(z)/T_s\) is not a ratio of polynomials and does not become a difference equation. We need an approximation. Three approximations of \(s\) They all come from approximating an integral \(\int x\,dt\) over one period: Forward Euler , a rectangle on the old sample: \(s \approx (z-1)/T_s\) . Backward Euler , a rectangle on the new sample: \(s \approx (z-1)/(zT_s)\) . Tustin , a trapezoid between the two: \[s = \frac{2}{T_s}\,\frac{z - 1}{z + 1} = \frac{2}{T_s}\,\frac{1 - z^{-1}}{1 + z^{-1}}\tag{1}\] ≡ Tustin is the only one of the three that maps the whole left half of the s-plane inside the unit circle and the \(j\omega\) axis exactly onto the circle. Backward Euler also preserves stability, but maps the \(j\omega\) axis onto a smaller circle inside the unit one; forward Euler can push a stable pole out of the circle. With Tustin, a stable continuous controller stays stable, and the frequency response is the same, only with the frequency axis warped. Frequency warping and prewarping Since the whole \(j\omega\) axis, out to infinity, is wrapped onto the circle up to \(f_s/2\) , the frequencies are compressed. The frequency \(\omega_d\) of the discrete controller reproduces what the continuous prototype did at \(\omega_a\) : \[\omega_a = \frac{2}{T_s}\tan\frac{\omega_d T_s}{2}, \qquad s = \frac{\omega_0}{\tan(\omega_0 T_s/2)}\,\frac{z - 1}{z + 1}\tag{2}\] ≡ Well below \(f_s/2\) , \(\tan x \approx x\) and the warping vanishes. Near \(f_s/2\) , it is strong. When one frequency matters, such as the crossover, the constant \(2/T_s\) is replaced with \(\omega_0/\tan(\omega_0 T_s/2)\) , the second part of (2) : the discrete response then agrees with the continuous one exactly at \(\omega_0\) . Prewarping It is choosing the bilinear transform's constant so that a chosen frequency \(\omega_0\) is reproduced without error. The others remain warped, less so near \(\omega_0\) . Matched poles and zeros Another way is not to approximate \(s\) , but to map each pole and each zero by the exact relation: a root at \(s = -\omega\) goes to \(z = e^{-\omega T_s}\) , and the integrator goes to \(z = 1\) . The gain is chosen afterwards, to cross where we want. This is the method of this site's 2p2z compensators ( The 2p2z compensator ): the Bode window computes \(K\) so that \(|T_L| = 1\) at the requested frequency, with the discrete controller already in place. title: Difference equation of the 2p2z
summary: The 2p2z compensator's difference equation, with the denominator in its general form; with the integrator at z = 1, it is the velocity form the firmware computes every period.
text: \[u[k] = -a_1\,u[k-1] - a_2\,u[k-2] + b_0\,e[k] + b_1\,e[k-1] + b_2\,e[k-2]\] \(u[k]\) is the duty computed in period \(k\) (stored already saturated), \(e[k]\) the error between the reference and the ADC sample, \(b_0\) , \(b_1\) , \(b_2\) the numerator's coefficients and \(a_1\) , \(a_2\) the denominator's, of \(C(z) = (b_0 + b_1 z^{-1} + b_2 z^{-2}) / (1 + a_1 z^{-1} + a_2 z^{-2})\) . With the integrator at \(z = 1\) and the pole \(p\) , the denominator is \((1 - z^{-1})(1 - p\,z^{-1})\) : \(a_1 = -(1 + p)\) and \(a_2 = p\) . Since \(1 + a_1 + a_2 = 0\) , the equation is the velocity form \(u[k] = u[k-1] + a_2\,(u[k-1] - u[k-2]) + b_0\,e[k] + b_1\,e[k-1] + b_2\,e[k-2]\) .

title: 2p2z compensator in z
summary: The two-pole, two-zero compensator, with its integrator at z = 1, written by its poles and zeros.
text: \[C(z) = K\,\frac{(1 - z_1 z^{-1})(1 - z_2 z^{-1})}{(1 - z^{-1})(1 - p\,z^{-1})}, \qquad z_i = e^{-\omega_{zi} T_s}, \quad p = e^{-\omega_p T_s}\] \(K\) is the gain, \(z_1\) and \(z_2\) the zeros, \(p\) the high-frequency pole and \(1 - z^{-1}\) the integrator. Expanded, \(C(z) = (b_0 + b_1 z^{-1} + b_2 z^{-2}) / (1 + a_1 z^{-1} + a_2 z^{-2})\) , with \(b_0 = K\) , \(b_1 = -K(z_1 + z_2)\) , \(b_2 = K z_1 z_2\) , \(a_1 = -(1 + p)\) and \(a_2 = p\) ; the zeros and the pole come from \(\omega_{z1}\) , \(\omega_{z2}\) and \(\omega_p\) by matching poles and zeros.

title: ADC step
summary: The ADC's step (LSB) referred to the converter's output, from the measuring range and the number of bits, including the resistive divider.
text: \[q = \frac{V_{FS}}{2^{N} - 1} = \frac{V_{\mathrm{ADC}}}{(2^{N} - 1)\,k_{\mathrm{div}}}\] \(q\) is the step (LSB) in volts at the output, \(N\) the number of bits, \(V_{FS}\) the measuring range referred to the output, \(V_{\mathrm{ADC}}\) the ADC's reference voltage at the pin (3.3 V on an STM32) and \(k_{\mathrm{div}} = v_{\mathrm{pin}}/v_o\) the ratio of the resistive divider. The \(2^N\) codes run from 0 to \(2^N - 1\) , and the largest one stands for full scale: there are \(2^N - 1\) steps between code 0 and the last, and code \(k\) reads \(k\,q\) .

title: \(G_{vd}(s)\) of the boost
summary: The transfer function from the duty to the output voltage of the boost in CCM, with losses, ESR and the right-half-plane zero.
text: \[G_{vd}(s) = Z_o(s)\,\frac{D' V - I\,(sL + R_l)}{sL + R_l + D'^2 Z_o(s)}, \qquad Z_o(s) = R \parallel \left(R_{ESR} + \frac{1}{sC}\right)\] \(D' = 1 - D\) , \(V\) is the output voltage, \(I\) the average inductor current, \(L\) the inductance, \(R_l\) the inductor's resistance plus one switch's, \(C\) and \(R_{ESR}\) the output capacitor and \(R\) the load. The numerator's \(-I(sL + R_l)\) term is the right-half-plane zero.

title: Duty ratio of the buck
summary: The ideal buck's duty ratio in CCM is the ratio of the output voltage to the input voltage.
text: \[D = \frac{V_o}{V_{in}}\] \(D\) is the fraction of the period \(T_s\) during which the high-side switch conducts, \(V_o\) is the average output voltage and \(V_{in}\) the input voltage. With the resistive losses \(R_s\) in series with the inductor, \(D\) rises slightly, to \((V_o + R_s I_o)/V_{in}\) .

title: \(G_{vd}(s)\) of the buck
summary: The transfer function from duty ratio to output voltage of the buck in CCM, in canonical form.
text: \[G_{vd}(s) = \frac{\hat v_o(s)}{\hat d(s)} = V_{in}\,\frac{R}{R + R_s}\;\frac{1 + s/\omega_{\mathrm{ESR}}}{1 + \dfrac{s}{Q\,\omega_0} + \dfrac{s^2}{\omega_0^2}}\] \(R\) is the load, \(R_s = R_L + R_{on}\) the resistance in series with the inductor, \(\omega_0\) and \(Q\) the LC filter's resonance and quality factor, and \(\omega_{\mathrm{ESR}} = 1/(R_{\mathrm{ESR}} C)\) the ESR zero. It does not include the digital loop's delay.

title: Inductor current ripple of the buck
summary: The peak-to-peak ripple of the buck's inductor current in CCM.
text: \[\Delta i_L = \frac{(V_{in} - V_o)\,D}{L\,f_s} = \frac{V_o\,(1 - D)}{L\,f_s}\] \(\Delta i_L\) is the peak-to-peak ripple, \(L\) the inductance and \(f_s = 1/T_s\) the switching frequency. The first form comes from the interval in which the switch conducts; the second, from the interval in which it is open.

title: Output voltage ripple of the buck
summary: The two parts of the buck's output ripple: the capacitor's and its ESR's.
text: \[\Delta v_C = \frac{\Delta i_L}{8\,C\,f_s}, \qquad \Delta v_{\mathrm{ESR}} = R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\,\Delta i_L\] \(\Delta v_C\) is the peak-to-peak ripple on the capacitance \(C\) , which absorbs the AC part of \(i_L\) ; \(\Delta v_{\mathrm{ESR}}\) is the drop on the capacitor's series resistance. The two are out of phase, so the total ripple lies between the larger one and their sum.

title: \(G_{vd}(s)\) of the four-switch buck-boost
summary: The transfer function from the duty to the output voltage of the four-switch buck-boost in buck-boost mode, in CCM, with losses and ESR.
text: \[G_{vd}(s) = Z_o(s)\,\frac{D'(V_{in} + V) - I\,(sL + R_l)}{sL + R_l + D'^2 Z_o(s)}, \qquad Z_o(s) = R \parallel \left(R_{ESR} + \frac{1}{sC}\right)\] \(D' = 1 - D\) , \(V_{in}\) and \(V\) are the input and output voltages, \(I\) the average inductor current, \(L\) the inductance, \(R_l\) the inductor's resistance plus those of the two switches always in series with it, \(C\) and \(R_{ESR}\) the output capacitor and \(R\) the load. It is the boost's plant with \(V_{in} + V\) in place of \(V\) : the voltage the duty switches across the inductor.

title: Right-half-plane zero of the buck-boost
summary: In the four-switch buck-boost, the right-half-plane zero depends on the load, on D' and on the ratio between the switched voltage, Vin + V, and the output.
text: \[\omega_{\mathrm{RHP}} = \frac{D'(V_{in} + V) - I R_l}{I L} \approx \frac{R\,D'^2}{L}\cdot\frac{V_{in} + V}{V}\] \(I = V/(R D')\) is the average inductor current, \(R\) the load, \(D' = 1 - D\) , \(L\) the inductance and \(R_l\) the series resistance of the inductor and the two switches. The approximation neglects the losses. With \(V_{in} + V\) replaced by \(V\) , it becomes the boost's again; the zero comes down when the load rises or the input falls.

title: Phase lost to the delay
summary: A pure delay leaves the loop gain's magnitude alone and takes a phase that grows linearly with frequency.
text: \[\varphi_d(f) = -360^\circ\, f\, t_d, \qquad t_d = (1 + D)\,T_s\] \(f\) is the frequency, \(t_d\) the total delay from the sample to the PWM edge it moves, \(D\) the duty and \(T_s\) the switching period. The value \((1 + D)\,T_s\) is this site's firmware's: update in the next period and a trailing-edge PWM.

title: DPWM resolution
summary: How many counts the timer makes in one PWM period, the duty step this allows and the equivalent number of bits.
text: \[N_{\mathrm{PWM}} = \frac{f_{\mathrm{clk}}}{f_s}, \qquad \Delta D = \frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{PWM}}}, \qquad n_{\mathrm{PWM}} = \log_2 N_{\mathrm{PWM}}\] \(f_{\mathrm{clk}}\) is the timer's effective counting frequency, \(f_s\) the switching frequency, \(N_{\mathrm{PWM}}\) the number of counts per period (up-counting; half that in center-aligned mode), \(\Delta D\) the smallest duty step and \(n_{\mathrm{PWM}}\) the resolution in bits.

title: ADC sample with the ESR
summary: In the boost and the buck-boost, the sample taken just before G1 turns on reads, besides the average output, the ESR drop of the part of the inductor current the average does not see.
text: \[\hat v_s = \hat v + R_{ESR}\left(D\,\hat i_L + I\,\hat d\right)\] \(\hat v_s\) is the perturbation of the ADC sample, \(\hat v\) that of the average output, \(\hat i_L\) and \(\hat d\) those of the inductor current and the duty, \(D\) and \(I\) the duty and the inductor current at the operating point, and \(R_{ESR}\) the capacitor's series resistance. It is the linearization of \(R_{ESR}\,d\,i_L\) : at the sampling instant, the capacitor receives the whole inductor current, \(d\,i_L\) more than the average \(d'\,i_L\) .

title: ESR zero
summary: The frequency of the zero that the output capacitor's series resistance adds to the plant.
text: \[f_{\mathrm{ESR}} = \frac{1}{2\pi\,R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\,C}\] \(R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\) is the capacitor's equivalent series resistance and \(C\) its capacitance. Above \(f_{\mathrm{ESR}}\) , the capacitor behaves as a resistor.

title: LC resonant frequency and quality factor
summary: The output filter's resonance and its quality factor, which depends on the load and the losses.
text: \[f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}, \qquad Q \approx \frac{1}{\dfrac{Z_0}{R} + \dfrac{R_s + R_{\mathrm{ESR}}}{Z_0}}, \qquad Z_0 = \sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}\] \(Z_0\) is the filter's characteristic impedance. The damping comes from the load \(R\) in parallel with the capacitor and from the series resistances \(R_s\) and \(R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\) ; the lighter the load (the larger \(R\) ), the higher the \(Q\) .

title: No-limit-cycle condition
summary: Peterchev and Sanders' conditions for a quantized loop to have a fixed point without a limit cycle, a DPWM finer than the ADC and an integrator of limited gain.
text: \[\Delta V_{\mathrm{DPWM}} = |G_{vd}(0)|\,\Delta D < q, \qquad 0 < k_i\,|G_{vd}(0)| \le 1\] \(|G_{vd}(0)|\) is the static gain from duty to output ( \(\approx V_{in}\) in the buck), \(\Delta D\) the DPWM step, \(q\) the ADC step and \(k_i\) how much the integrator changes the duty per sample for each volt of error; the first condition asks for a DPWM finer than the ADC, and the second for an integrator ( \(k_i > 0\) ) of limited gain. The product \(k_i\,|G_{vd}(0)|\) is Peterchev and Sanders' integral gain \(K_i\) , with the variables normalized to \(V_{in}\) : with \(K_i \le 1\) , one code of error moves the output, through the integrator, by at most one ADC step per sample.

title: Loop gain
summary: The loop gain is the product of the controller, the plant and the sensor, taken once around the loop.
text: \[T_L(s) = G_c(s)\,G_{vd}(s)\,H\] \(G_c\) is the controller (duty per volt of error), \(G_{vd}\) is the plant from the duty to the output voltage, including the digital loop's delays, and \(H\) is the sensor's gain, in measured volts per volt of output.

title: Averaged switching cell of the buck
summary: The buck's switch pair, averaged over one period, becomes an ideal transformer of ratio 1 : d.
text: \[\langle v_{sw} \rangle_{T_s} = d\,\langle v_{in} \rangle_{T_s}, \qquad \langle i_{in} \rangle_{T_s} = d\,\langle i_L \rangle_{T_s}\] \(v_{sw}\) is the switching-node voltage, \(i_{in}\) the current drawn from the input, \(d\) the duty ratio and \(\langle x \rangle_{T_s}\) the moving average of \(x\) over one switching period.

title: RMS current in the buck's output capacitor
summary: The RMS current in the buck's output capacitor in CCM, which is the triangular part of the inductor current.
text: \[I_{C,\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{\Delta i_L}{\sqrt{12}}\] \(\Delta i_L\) is the peak-to-peak ripple of the inductor current. It holds for a triangular wave of any duty ratio, assuming a constant load current.

title: Prewarping
summary: The bilinear transform's frequency warping, and the constant that cancels it at a chosen frequency.
text: \[\omega_a = \frac{2}{T_s}\tan\frac{\omega_d T_s}{2}, \qquad s = \frac{\omega_0}{\tan(\omega_0 T_s/2)}\,\frac{z - 1}{z + 1}\] \(\omega_d\) is the discrete controller's frequency, \(\omega_a\) the continuous prototype's frequency it reproduces, \(T_s\) the sampling period and \(\omega_0\) the frequency where the two agree after prewarping, usually the crossover.

title: Q15 format
summary: How a 16-bit integer represents a fractional number in the Qm.n format, and how two of them are multiplied with rounding.
text: \[x = \frac{X}{2^{n}}, \quad X \in \left[-2^{m+n},\; 2^{m+n}-1\right], \qquad Z = \left\lfloor \frac{X\,Y + 2^{n-1}}{2^{n}} \right\rfloor\] \(X\) is the stored integer, \(x\) the value it represents, \(m\) the integer bits besides the sign and \(n\) the fraction bits; Q15 is \(m = 0\) , \(n = 15\) , from \(-1\) to \(1 - 2^{-15}\) . \(Z\) is the product of \(X\) and \(Y\) , both with \(n\) fraction bits, rounded and brought back to \(n\) fraction bits.

title: Right-half-plane zero of the boost
summary: The frequency of the boost's right-half-plane zero falls with the square of D' and with the load current.
text: \[\omega_{\mathrm{RHP}} = \frac{R\,D'^2 - R_l}{L} \approx \frac{R\,D'^2}{L}\] \(R\) is the load, \(D' = 1 - D\) , \(L\) the inductance and \(R_l\) the series resistance of the inductor and one switch. The approximation neglects the losses; the zero comes down when the load rises (smaller \(R\) ) or the input falls (smaller \(D'\) ).

title: Bilinear transform
summary: The bilinear (Tustin) transform replaces s with a ratio of polynomials in z, like integrating by the trapezoidal rule.
text: \[s = \frac{2}{T_s}\,\frac{z - 1}{z + 1} = \frac{2}{T_s}\,\frac{1 - z^{-1}}{1 + z^{-1}}\] \(T_s\) is the sampling period. It maps the left half of the s-plane inside the unit circle of z, and the \(j\omega\) axis onto the circle.

title: Zero-order hold
summary: The zero-order hold keeps each sample for one period, which amounts to an average delay of half a period.
text: \[G_h(s) = \frac{1 - e^{-sT_s}}{s}, \qquad \frac{G_h(j\omega)}{T_s} = \frac{\sin(\omega T_s/2)}{\omega T_s/2}\, e^{-j\omega T_s/2}\] \(T_s\) is the sampling period and \(\omega\) the angular frequency. The magnitude, normalized by \(T_s\) , is a sinc function, and the phase is \(-\omega T_s/2\) : half a period of delay.
